https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text: MPs socialise on the terrace outside the House of Commons. Politicians have described how alcohol is readily available throughout the day, including at daytime lobbying events. Photograph: Mark Kerrison/In Pictures/Getty View image in fullscreen MPs socialise on the terrace outside the House of Commons. Politicians have described how alcohol is readily available throughout the day, including at daytime lobbying events. Photograph: Mark Kerrison/In Pictures/Getty Politics ‘MPs have had their stomachs pumped’: concerns over ‘alcohol-soaked’ culture in Westminster Alcohol is embedded in profession where long hours, loneliness and lobbying are the norm, report finds Denis Campbell Sat 1 Aug 2026 03.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 04.40 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Parliament is “Britain’s last alcohol-soaked workplace” where MPs are offered free drinks as early as midday despite alcohol-related scandals, a report has reveal ed. Drinking is commonplace and some MPs have had their stomachs pumped after consuming so much alcohol that they ended up in hospital, one disclosed. Alcohol is “embedded” in how Westminster works, driven by loneliness among MPs, socialising in order to meet ministers, and drinks being served at daytime and evening events. View image in fullscreen The Churchill Room bar on the terrace of the House of Commons. Photograph: Lisa Ryder/Alamy Those are the findings of a survey of 190 MPs and their staff which shows that Westminster’s drinking culture endures, despite rising concern and a string of incidents, including an MP’s researcher allegedly having had her drink spiked in Strangers’ bar in parliament and the revelation that the Labour MP Neil Coyle was at one time drinking up to 200 units of alcohol a week – the equivalent of 10 pints a night. The spiking led to a police investigation and the temporary closure of Strangers’ bar. The report, by the Institute of Alcohol Studies (IAS) thinktank, said: “The findings suggest that Westminster remains a highly unusual workplace where alcohol is embedded in professional life, networking, lobbying and socialising in ways that would be exceptional in most other UK workplaces. View image in fullscreen Andy Burnham and the chancellor, John Healey, visit a pub during a trip to Essex. The report found alcohol was embedded in networking, lobbying and socialising for those working in Westminster. Photograph: Richard Pohle/Pool Times Media Ltd/AP “Participants described alcohol as being available throughout the working day, frequently provided for free, and often intertwined with career advancement.” Twenty-four MPs, 58 Westminster staff and 108 constituency office personnel shared their experiences and views. One MP, describing how readily available alcohol was at Westminster, said: “Going to a meeting at noon and alcohol’s available. Of course, I’m not used to that in my old job.” The free alcohol at events on the parliamentary estate, which organisations arrange to help them lobby MPs, emerged as a particular issue. Another MP said: “Where else in a work environment would you go, unless it was the works Christmas do, and there was free alcohol there for you? It just wouldn’t happen in real life.” A third said: “You can start drinking here from 12 o’clock onwards and go around and consume large amounts of alcohol, and it’s relatively freely available.” A fourth described events as a “legitimised opportunity to drink alcohol”, while a fifth said this routine provision of alcohol helps to create a “casual attitude to drinking”. Hannah Spencer, the Green party MP elected at the Gorton and Denton byelection in February, received a mixed reaction from MPs when in April she labelled Westminster’s drinking culture “unprofessional and worrying” and said it led to cases of “questionable and dangerous behaviour”. She remarked that “you can smell the alcohol when people are in between votes”. View image in fullscreen Hannah Spencer said she found Westminster’s drinking culture ‘unprofessional and worrying’ after being elected as an MP this year. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian The IAS report also found that: 42% of the MPs interviewed had been offered an alcoholic drink at a work meeting or event on a weekly basis during the previous six months; 13% said that occurred daily. 22% had concerns about a colleague’s drinking. Parliament’s long and unusual working hours, the loneliness many MPs experience being away from home, the pressures of the job and socialising in order to advance their careers can all act as catalysts for drinking. The report added: “The availability of alcohol was seen to encourage unhealthy behaviour in general, from affecting colleagues’ sleep and stress levels to potentially normalising high-risk drinking, with one MP referring to colleagues having had their stomachs pumped in hospital and going back into Westminster the following day.” Some MPs said the findings should prompt Westminster to rethink its attitude to alcohol. The Labour MP Cat Smith said: “We wouldn’t accept a surgeon operating after a drink or a driver getting behind the wheel – so why should we accept legislators voting on the laws of the land after one? “If we’re serious about being a professional workplace, we have to ask hard questions about practices like late night votes that sit alongside on-tap bars.” Beccy Cooper, who was a public health consultant before entering parliament as a Labour MP in 2024, said the report was a wake-up call. In a foreword to the report, she suggested that parliament should draw up its first formal workplace policy on alcohol. She added: “Two findings stood out to me. Almost one in 10 respondents reported a negative experience because of someone else’s drinking at work and 70% either didn’t know, or weren’t sure, how to raise a concern about a colleague’s drinking. “That combination – real, measurable harm and no clear route to address it – is exactly the kind of gap we need to address.” View image in fullscreen Some MPs said Westminster should rethink its attitude to alcohol and parts of the job such as late night votes that sit alongside bars on-site. Photograph: House of Commons/PA Katherine Severi, the IAS’s chief executive, said Westminster should limit the provision of free alcohol to evening events as part of a renewed drive to make it a more modern workplace, which many MPs and staff support. “Very few professions these days would allow free alcohol from midday, or regularly host outside organisations sponsoring events where drinking is the norm during working hours,” she added. The report also said that the commercialisation of parliament as an events venue contributed to MPs’ drinking. In 2023, parliament’s independent complaints and grievance scheme said alcohol was a “frequent factor” in its investigations into alleged misconduct at Westminster. In its findings of 30 investigations it undertook between 2021 and 2022, it added that drinking in parliament’s array of bars was “leading to intimidating behaviour like shouting and swearing”. In July 2023, Daniel Greenberg, the parliamentary standards commissioner, said alcohol had led to “behaviour problems” at Westminster and suggested the sale of alcohol on the state be kept under review. A parliament spokesperson said everyone working there had been reminded to use alcohol responsibly, but hinted that immediate changes were unlikely. “Any changes to parliament’s provision of alcohol would ultimately be a matter for members to decide on. The estate is a unique working environment that includes public access and events,” they said. “Parliament’s behaviour code makes clear that everyone should be treated with respect at all times, and those who choose to drink alcohol on the estate must do so responsibly.” Westminster’s efforts to promote more responsible drinking include greater provision of no- and low-alcohol products and venue staff’s right to refuse to serve anyone who is, or looks likely to become, intoxicated. https://www.politico.eu/article/andy-bur.text: LONDON — Andy Burnham will welcome French President Emmanuel Macron to Downing Street next week as he intensifies his diplomatic efforts with Britain’s closest allies. Macron will attend the formal opening of the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition at the British Museum, where the 900-year-old artifact is being displayed on loan as a gesture of friendship between the two countries, according to two people briefed on the plans. He is also expected to take part in a bilateral meeting with the British prime minister. It is the first U.K. visit by an EU leader of Burnham’s tenure and coincides with the return of the U.K. parliament after the summer recess. Advertisement Advertisement A U.K. government official, granted anonymity because they were not authorized to speak on the record, said Burnham is looking forward to welcoming Macron to Downing Street. The Elysée declined to confirm the trip. It follows Burnham’s recent trip to Kyiv to mark Ukraine’s independence day, which saw him meet Volodymyr Zelenskyy and pledge closer support to equip Ukraine with blueprints for Storm Shadow long-range missiles, allowing Ukraine to manufacture components for the weapon domestically. Britain’s new prime minister has focused heavily on domestic issues such as the cost of living and a shortage of prison spaces in the weeks since he took office, but his recent diplomatic blitz shows he is determined to signal continued solidarity with the U.K.’s key allies. In one of his first calls to international counterparts, Burnham told Macron he was “looking forward to building” on “the strong U.K.-France relationship to deliver for people on both sides of the Channel.” Continuing work on the “reset” of relations between London and Brussels begun under Keir Starmer is likely to be high on their agenda, together with tackling illegal migration. Advertisement Advertisement Burnham told António Costa, the president of the European Council, the U.K. must be “bolder” about moving closer to the EU as the pair met en route to Kyiv earlier this week, but has not given any indication he will move away from the red lines set in the last Labour manifesto. The U.K. and EU are due to hold a summit in October after one originally planned for July was postponed due to Starmer’s resignation. The two sides are hoping to reach an agreement on the thorny topic of tuition fees at the meeting, alongside an agri-food deal to smooth trade, an emissions trading arrangement and a youth mobility scheme to make it easier for young people to live abroad. Dan Bloom and Clea Caulcutt contributed to this report.

https://www.politico.eu/article/german-l.text: Top lawmakers in the European Parliament want to replace the fragile alliance supporting Ursula von der Leyen with a formal German-style centrist coalition — over fears her group relies too much on the far right to pass legislation. Niclas Herbst and René Repasi, the respective parliamentary leaders of Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s center-right Christian Democrats and Vice Chancellor Lars Klingbeil’s center-left Social Democrats — the two parties that govern Germany — said they want their pan-European political families to strike a deal to push through policies as a united front rather than bicker over issues they disagree on. In what would be a striking reversal of how their two groups have drifted apart, they want formal governance structures to resolve disputes and take turns promoting their priorities. “If we don’t have trust, and if we don’t find good solutions, if we do not deliver for the people, the populists and extremists on the left and on the right will decide,” Herbst said, sitting in an armchair next to Repasi, in the center-left lawmaker’s office during a joint interview — itself a stunning case of two rival politicians wanting to put their differences aside to fight what they see as a common enemy. According to a POLITICO poll of polls , the three centrist groups are on course to lose 49 seats at the next election. Advertisement The far right’s gains in the 2024 EU election disrupted the longstanding balance between the two political groups that drove lawmaking for decades. The EPP, of which the CDU is a member, has increasingly relied on right-wing majorities due to fraying cooperation with the S&D, to which the German Social Democrats belong. With polls signaling further populist gains across the bloc, Herbst and Repasi warned that unless the center repairs the relationship, more extreme voices will increasingly call the shots in Brussels. The Herbst-Repasi idea would also help reduce European Commission President von der Leyen’s political stress. Rivalry between the two centrist groups has made Parliament votes on some of her biggest policies increasingly unpredictable ― such as in January when MEPs sent her EU-Mercosur trade deal for judicial review. A coalition agreement would restore stability, giving the Commission and capitals greater confidence in Parliament’s ability to deliver von der Leyen’s program, the MEPs said. Continued “frustration” and “distrust” stemming from the EPP striking deals with the far-right could eventually drive the two groups completely apart, triggering a “political catastrophe” because the whole Brussels system would be paralyzed, Repasi said. ‘Basis of trust’ With far-right and far-left forces on track to make major gains at the 2029 EU election, Herbst warned that failing to work together would give “even more ammunition to the populists from the left and the right,”allowing them to keep scoring “easy wins” in Parliament. “If mistrust continues, it will only be amplified by the 2029 elections,” his center-left counterpart added. “The need to talk to each other is going to be even bigger.” He said a potential pact could serve as the “model” for the next legislature. Since June 2024, the EPP has increasingly joined forces with far-right groups to pass key legislation, including on deportations, cuts to green reporting requirements for businesses, and delays and rollbacks to a deforestation law. The group has also relied on far-right votes to shape the agenda in Parliament’s decision-making bodies. Advertisement Borrowing from the German model, the two MEPs said the two main groups should work together more formally and no longer rely on negotiations file-by-file by individual lawmakers. “If a trade-off is not possible within a file, we need to find a trade-off across files,” Repasi said. Partners need to agree on concessions that are “difficult to digest” for each other. This would create “this joint feeling of mutual trust.” Compromises on which group gets the leading voice in different areas could be struck across files in advance, giving the two sides an incentive to stick together. The two MEPs also floated the idea of creating a new “governance structure” body to steer coalition disputes and allocate who gets which win, similar to the coalition committee between the CDU and SPD in Berlin. Ursula von der Leyen delivers a speech during a plenary session at the Strasbourg European Parliament on May 20, 2026. | Sebastien Bozon/AFP via Getty Images “We need more binding agreements on who will take the lead on which question,” said Herbst, who defended a deal but rejected the term ‘coalition,’ arguing it has different meanings across the EU. “Everybody needs to have some successes.” The EPP is the biggest group and hence needs to get its fair share of “wins,” though, he said. Will it happen? Whether Herbst and Repasi’s plan has legs depends on political will across the two groups — and there doesn’t appear to be much. “This is nothing new,” said a spokesperson for S&D chief Iratxe García. “It was already on the negotiation table in 2024.” Advertisement A spokesperson for EPP head Manfred Weber didn’t reply to a request for comment. Herbst said Weber could be open to a broader deal, provided it reflected the rightward shift seen at the 2024 EU election. After that vote, the two groups, along with liberal Renew, signed a two-page agreement vaguely promising to cooperate. That didn’t prevent the EPP from working with the far-right. The plan’s key weakness is that lawmakers have fewer incentives to follow the party line than national lawmakers. Unlike in countries, Parliament cannot be dissolved and failure to maintain a majority does not bring down the Commission. Members of the European parliament take part in an electronical vote. | Jean-Christophe Verhaegen/AFP via Getty Images That problem was on display when an EPP-S&D deal to cut red tape for businesses collapsed in October when center-left MEPs rebelled against their leadership, prompting the EPP to vote with the far-right. Involving more MEPs in coalition negotiations would create greater ownership and discipline among lawmakers, Repasi said. In thinly veiled criticism of the groups’ leadership, he argued that the “previous way of how politics was done by two or three people at the very top that decided everything has just come to its limits.” Forced together Despite the two groups’ growing mistrust, they will soon have to find common ground on issues such as plans to water down a combustion-engine ban, a package simplifying environmental rules, including the contentious emissions trading system, a revamp of the EU border agency, Frontex, and the EU’s notoriously thorny seven-year budget. Advertisement “You might have some success with the far left or the far right on certain issues, but in the bigger picture we have far more in common with liberals and social democrats,” Herbst said. There’s also the matter of who gets the Parliament presidency. MEPs expect the EPP’s Roberta Metsola to seek a third term as president, but the S&D insist it’s their turn. Failure to find a common candidate would expose the proposed centrist pact’s weakness before it even gets off the ground, Repasi said. Herbst agreed the two groups should agree on a common candidate. The German tradition The proposal comes as the leadership of both groups tries to beef up informal relations between top lawmakers, following souring relations between the two chiefs, Weber and García. Asked why they were taking the initiative rather than relying on the group leaders, both pointed to Germany’s long tradition of grand coalitions. “It is good that those who have made positive experiences with this sort of governance try to translate it into the European level … and therefore the impulse is coming from the two German heads of delegations,” Repasi said. Herbst said he hadn’t directly consulted with Merz about the coalition plan, but that it was important to Berlin to have “good cooperation.” For his part, Klingbeil has been “informed” of the initiative, Repasi said, adding “it is also in the interest of the German government” that things agreed in Berlin are followed through in the EU Parliament. “Let’s not talk too much about the past or personal relationships but look to the future,” Herbst said. https://www.thetimes.com/life-style/luxu.text: Accessibility Links From Matisse to Picasso, the secret stories of artist friendships We know all about artist rivalries, but a new exhibition looks at the friendships that have influenced the life and work of those such as Francis Bacon and Pablo Picasso Caziel, right, with his friend and mentor Picasso, whom he met in 1948 Whitford Fine Art Louisa McKenzie Thursday September 10 2026, 4.10am BST , The Times Listen 0:00 / • 8:46 min Share Share this article Email Twitter Facebook Link Save Puzzles Challenge yourself with today's puzzles. There cannot have been many visits to Francis Bacon’s famously chaotic studio at 7 Reece Mews in London that ended with Bacon’s face covered in plaster and two straws protruding from his nostrils. Yet that was the situation in which the sculptor Clive Barker found himself in 1969. Barker — not to be confused with the horror writer of the same name — had decided that he wanted to make a life mask of his friend. Bacon agreed. Barker arrived at the cramped South Kensington studio with an experimental lightweight plaster mixture, covered Bacon’s face and inserted the straws so that he could breathe. Throughout the process, Barker held Bacon’s hand: if anything went wrong, Bacon could squeeze it and the plaster would come off. “After I had successfully completed the cast, he told me he had been in agony because of his asthma,” Barker later explained of the mask, a gilded bronze cast of which can be viewed at London’s National Portrait Gallery. “I felt terrible, but very touched by Francis’s support.” Luxury newsletter The inside track on tech, travel, philanthropy and the hottest handbags, cars and spas. Sign up with one click You’ve successfully signed up to the Luxury newsletter Explore our newsletters An error occurred. Please use the link below. Luxury newsletter Explore our newsletters It is an unusually intimate image of one of the most formidable figures in postwar art. It is also a reminder of the support between artists that could lie behind the making of art: sitting in one another’s studios, borrowing ideas, arguing about paintings, holidaying together and, occasionally, even proposing marriage. This is the subject of Artists and Their Inspirations , a presentation by Whitford Fine Art at the British Art Fair , which returns to the Saatchi Gallery from September 24-27. The gallery has drawn on artists’ estates to explore three relationships: Mildred Bendall and Henri Matisse; the Polish-born painter Caziel and Pablo Picasso; and Barker and Bacon. Top stories 1 Dolly Parton’s ‘arms dealer’ nephew sacked in row over her estate US news 2 Meet the Times reader with more passport stamps than the Travel desk Inspiration “At Whitford Fine Art, we are particularly interested in artists whose work has not always received the recognition it deserves, and in understanding the circumstances that shaped both their careers and their work,” explains An Jo Fermon, the director of Whitford Fine Art. “Mildred Bendall’s achievements were too often overlooked in the context of a male-dominated art world, while Clive Barker was an artist who never sought the limelight or actively promoted his own work. Caziel, meanwhile, deliberately resisted the commercialisation of his art. Yet all three developed significant relationships with artists of their generation, and those exchanges left a lasting mark.” Pansies, c 1950, by Mildred Bendall Whitford Fine Art Mildred Bendall painting at the Port of Oleron Whitford Fine Art The least familiar name may be Bendall’s. Born in Bordeaux in 1891 to an English father and French mother, Mildred Bendall was an accomplished draughtswoman who moved to Paris in the late 1920s following her admission to the influential exhibition the Salon des Artistes Français. She thus entered the orbit of Matisse, then at the peak of his career. Their friendship changed her painting. Matisse’s great lesson, through his Fauvism, was that colour need not obediently fill spaces created by drawing: colour itself could create form and space. Bendall began dispensing with dark outlines and building her pictures through blocks of colour instead. Her Still Life with Pansies , painted around 1950 and appearing at the fair, is a good example of this. The vase of flowers becomes evidence of a conversation begun decades earlier in Paris — and of the way an artistic idea can migrate from one person to another. Advertisement The relationship became personal. Bendall was a frequent visitor to the Matisse household and became so close to the family that Matisse’s son Paul proposed marriage. She turned him down and subsequently returned to Bordeaux. Bendall might not have taken Matisse’s son, but she took Matisse’s ideas with her, cofounding the group Artistes indépendents bordelais in 1928. She encouraged younger artists to create volume through colour rather than the academic convention of adding black and white. Her leadership of the group saw artists such as Braque, Utrillo and Picasso — as well as her mentor Matisse — participate in its annual exhibitions. Port of Oleron, 1953, by Mildred Bendall Whitford Fine Art The relationship between Caziel and Picasso was more reciprocal still. Caziel, born Kazimierz Zielenkiewicz in Poland in 1906, arrived in Paris before the war. His stay in Paris had been in part facilitated by another great artist — Édouard Vuillard, best known for his colourful domestic scenes. During the war, Caziel and his Jewish wife, the painter Lutka Pink, found refuge in Aix-en-Provence. In 1948 the Polish government gave Caziel, then established in Paris, a peculiar errand: he was to deliver to Picasso a traditional Polish coat made from the pelt of black heath sheep. Top stories 1 Gunmen kill 11 at house party in South Africa Africa 2 London stock market set for biggest flotation in five years Companies & Markets Caziel duly appeared at Picasso’s studio in the Rue des Grands Augustins in Paris. The two hit it off. Both were expatriates; both understood what it meant to be separated from their homeland, and they shared an enthusiasm for Polish folk art. Then Caziel noticed something extraordinary in the studio. Picasso was working on a portrait of his young son, Claude — and had based it on a design Caziel had made for the catalogue of the 1948 Unesco exhibition. For an artist meeting Picasso, it must have been a startling reversal of expectations: the most famous painter alive had already borrowed from him. Still Life with Peaches, 1936, by Caziel Whitford Fine Art The friendship continued. Between 1948 and 1952 the two men spent summers together at Juan les Pins on the Côte d’Azur, drawing caricatures of each other. Picasso’s influenced Caziel’s paintings, while Caziel simultaneously pushed towards abstraction. Then came an opportunity most painters in Paris would have found almost impossible to refuse. Daniel-Henry Kahnweiler, Picasso’s dealer, invited Caziel to join his stable. There was a catch. Kahnweiler regarded Caziel’s experiments with abstraction as just that — experiments —and expected him to return to figurative painting. Caziel said no. Most commented 1 Andy Burnham hopes to clinch EU reset deal by end of the year Politics 659 comments By 1951 he had largely abandoned figuration and joined Groupe Espace, which sought to bring constructivist art and architecture together. Caziel remained committed to abstraction for the rest of his career. It makes the relationship with Picasso considerably more interesting than a simple tale of mentor and mentee: Picasso helped Caziel find freedom, and Caziel exercised that freedom by going somewhere his mentor would not follow. This year marks the 120th anniversary of Caziel’s birth, making the fair’s presentation an opportunity to reconsider an artist who stood remarkably close to the centre of European modernism without becoming a household name. Advertisement Clive Barker, right, with Francis Bacon in his Reece Mews studio Whitford Fine Art Clive Barker’s Study of Francis Bacon No 3 Whitford Fine Art Barker and Bacon offer a different sort of relationship again. Barker was more than three decades younger than Bacon, but theirs is better understood as friendship and mutual fascination than conventional mentorship. Barker made 12 bronze portrait studies of Bacon. Bacon, in turn, painted Barker. Barker’s sculptures became increasingly extraordinary. In Francis Bacon (1909–1992), Study No 6 (Head and Teeth) , he incorporated casts of real teeth and tubing suggesting a windpipe. The polished sculpture seems almost infected by Bacon’s own imagery: the mouth, flesh and vulnerable human body that obsessively recur in Bacon’s paintings have migrated into Barker’s sculpture. The exchange eventually became explicit. In 1978 an exhibition at the Felicity Samuel Gallery in London paired 12 Studies of Francis Bacon by Barker with 3 Studies of Clive Barker by Bacon. One artist looked at the other, and the other looked back. This perhaps explains the fascination of these three relationships. They transgress the romantic mythology of the solitary genius. Matisse gave Bendall a new way of thinking about colour, but she passed it on to her own circle of acolytes. Picasso influenced Caziel, but also borrowed from him. Barker studied Bacon’s face so closely that he covered it in plaster; Bacon responded in his own medium, paint. The works at the British Art Fair tell stories not just of influences but of encounters: a rejected marriage proposal; a Polish sheepskin coat; summers spent making caricatures on the Riviera and two breathing straws poking through wet plaster. These vignettes from everyday life had a profound effect on some of the 20th century’s most interesting art. Grzegorz Braun, member of far-right political alliance Confederation, speaks during a session at the Parliament in Warsaw, Poland, Dec. 12, 2023. Photo: REUTERS/Aleksandra Szmigiel Karol Nawrocki, Poland’s president, is a historian whom Donald Trump calls “my friend” and whom Russia has placed on its wanted list. Grzegorz Braun, a far-right politician notorious for antisemitism, calls the Auschwitz gas chambers “fake.” Weeks after the Bucha massacre, he said he would not rush to label Vladimir Putin a criminal. On Saturday, recordings were released in which Braun calls Nawrocki’s office a “Judenrat.” “We are corresponding with a Judenrat. We are not corresponding with a Polish president, but with a Judenrat,” Braun says. The country’s highest state institutions, he adds, “represent an occupying power over Poles.” Braun has made clear who he believes runs Poland. In 2020, from the floor of parliament, he described the country as a “Russian-German condominium, under Jewish trusteeship,” adding that today “one should say: Jewish-American.” Later that year, when parliament debated a defense cooperation agreement with Washington, he called it “Colonization Plus, or maybe even Occupation Plus.” In Braun’s political imagination, antisemitism and anti-Americanism are parts of the same story about an occupied Poland. On Sept. 23, 1939, with Warsaw still under German siege, the city’s mayor, Stefan Starzyński, appointed an engineer named Adam Czerniaków to lead its Jewish community. On Oct. 4, days after the city surrendered, the Germans made him head of the Judenrat. For nearly three years, Czerniaków bargained with the occupiers over food, forced labor, and exemptions, and kept a diary. On July 22, 1942, the SS ordered the council to deliver 6,000 people a day for “resettlement to the East.” He tried to save the children of the ghetto’s orphanages and failed. The next day, he swallowed cyanide in his office on Grzybowska Street. “They are demanding that I kill the children of my people with my own hands,” he wrote to his wife. “There is nothing left for me but to die.” Eighty-four years later, a Polish member of the European Parliament has turned the name of Czerniaków’s council into an insult for the office of Poland’s president. The recordings, released by the Polish YouTube channel PRZEkanał, capture Braun, leader of the Confederation of the Polish Crown, complaining that the president’s office had brushed off the people his party proposed for presidential advisory councils. “The president’s office completely blew off our noble candidates,” he says. Its officials are “lowlifes” who did not send “so much as an email.” Moscow gets gentler treatment. Four weeks before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, on Jan. 27, 2022, Poland’s lower house voted 456-1 for a resolution backing Kyiv. The one vote against was Braun’s. On June 11 of this year, Piotr Heszen, who runs the office of Braun’s parliamentary group, attended a reception at the Russian Embassy in Warsaw. He argued for “normalization of relations with our Russian neighbor” and confirmed that he had cleared the visit with Braun. In March, Braun signed the condolence book at Iran’s embassy for Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, a man who had called Israel a “cancerous tumor.” US Ambassador Tom Rose replied on X: “How disgusting.” The antisemitism is not subtle. In July 2025, Braun told Radio Wnet, a conservative station, that “Auschwitz with gas chambers is, unfortunately, fake.” The host, Łukasz Jankowski, ended the interview on the spot: “There are certain limits.” In August, prosecutors from the Institute of National Remembrance the state body Nawrocki led until he became president, charged Braun on two counts of denying Nazi crimes at Auschwitz-Birkenau. In November 2025, speaking in Oświęcim, near the former Auschwitz-Birkenau camp, Braun said that Poland is for Poles and that other nations, including the Jews, have their own countries. Nawrocki has chosen Washington. Russia placed him on its wanted list over his campaign to remove Soviet-era monuments while he led the Institute. On May 21, announcing 5,000 additional US troops for Poland, Trump pointed to Nawrocki’s election and noted that he had endorsed him. On Sept. 17, he credited “the bold leadership of my friend, Karol Nawrocki” for what he described as progress toward a US Army base in Poland. Nawrocki has said he wants the base to be permanent and would like it to be called Fort Trump. Trump’s ambassador in Warsaw is Rose, an Orthodox Jew and a former publisher of The Jerusalem Post. Before the runoff, Braun announced that he would vote for Nawrocki. According to exit polling, 92.5 percent of Braun’s first-round voters who returned for the runoff also voted for Nawrocki. Braun now calls the office of the president he backed a “Judenrat.” Braun is not a fringe curiosity. He won 6.3 percent in last year’s presidential election, and in a September poll by United Surveys for the news site Wirtualna Polska, his party stood at 10.9 percent. Yet Jarosław Kaczyński, who leads Law and Justice, Poland’s largest opposition party, has ruled out a governing coalition with Braun even if that means staying out of government. In February, Rose told the Polish daily Rzeczpospolita that Braun is “very anti-American” and that a government including his party would be “a serious problem” for the United States. For Braun, a Poland allied with Washington is a Poland under occupation. Trump calls Nawrocki “my friend.” Braun calls Nawrocki’s office a “Judenrat.” Washington calls the relationship an alliance.
